Symptom: Dizziness
A Public Health Awareness Reference
Symptom Overview
Dizziness is a general term for feeling unsteady, light-headed, or like the surroundings are spinning. Some people feel like they may faint, others feel off-balance while standing or walking, and some feel a spinning sensation known as vertigo. Dizziness may last a few seconds, come and go, or continue for a longer time. It can happen suddenly while standing up, during physical activity, or without any clear trigger.
Dizziness is a symptom, not a disease by itself. It can be caused by many different things, from mild and temporary reasons to conditions that need medical attention. This document does not identify which condition you may have. It only offers general, safe information to help you understand dizziness as a symptom and decide your next steps.
Possible Common Causes
Dizziness can happen for many reasons. Some common and general possibilities include:
Dehydration or heat exposure: Not drinking enough water, sweating heavily, or spending long hours in strong heat can lower fluid and salt levels and cause dizziness.
Low blood pressure: Standing up too quickly, especially after sitting or lying down, can briefly reduce blood flow to the brain and cause light-headedness.
Low blood sugar: Skipping meals or going without food for long periods can cause weakness, shakiness, and dizziness.
Anaemia (low blood count): Ongoing tiredness and dizziness can happen when the body does not have enough healthy red blood cells, often linked to poor diet.
Inner ear problems: Conditions affecting the inner ear's balance system can cause a spinning sensation (vertigo), sometimes with nausea.
Motion sickness: Travel by road, boat, or on rough terrain can cause temporary dizziness and nausea in some people.
Stress, anxiety, or poor sleep: Emotional strain, overwork, or lack of rest can sometimes bring on light-headedness.
Side effects of medicines: Certain medicines, including those for blood pressure or sedation, can cause dizziness as a side effect.
This list is general and not complete. It is not possible to know the exact cause of dizziness from a description alone. A trained health worker or doctor needs to examine and, where needed, test the person to understand the cause.
Self-Care Advice
For mild, brief dizziness with no other worrying symptoms, the following general steps may help:
Sit or lie down immediately when you feel dizzy, to avoid a fall or injury.
Rise slowly from sitting or lying down, rather than standing up suddenly.
Drink water, ORS (oral rehydration solution), or a fluid with a pinch of salt and sugar, especially in hot weather or after sweating heavily.
Rest in a cool, shaded, well-ventilated place if the dizziness may be linked to heat.
Eat regular meals and avoid going for long hours without food.
Avoid sudden head movements or quick changes in position until the dizziness passes.
Avoid driving, climbing, operating machinery, or working near heights or fire while feeling dizzy.
If dizziness is mild and passes within a few minutes with rest and fluids, continue to observe yourself over the next day for repeat episodes.
When to Seek Medical Attention
Visit the nearest health sub-centre, Ayushman Arogya Mandir, primary health centre (PHC), or hospital promptly if dizziness occurs along with any of the following:
Fainting or loss of consciousness, even briefly.
Chest pain, pounding or irregular heartbeat, or difficulty breathing.
Sudden weakness or numbness in the face, arm, or leg, especially on one side of the body.
Slurred speech, confusion, difficulty understanding others, or trouble seeing.
Severe headache that comes on suddenly and is unlike any headache before.
Repeated vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down.
A fall or head injury linked to the dizzy spell.
Dizziness with high fever, severe dehydration, or signs of heat stroke, such as very hot skin, confusion, or not sweating despite heat.
Dizziness that is severe, does not improve with rest, keeps returning, or is getting worse over time.
Dizziness in a pregnant woman, elderly person, small child, or someone with a known heart condition, diabetes, or high blood pressure.
If any of the above signs are present, do not wait — seek medical help immediately, or call the emergency helpline (108 or 102) for urgent transport and care.
Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha experiences intense heat waves, especially between March and June, when temperatures can rise sharply. Health authorities have flagged dizziness, weakness, and fainting as early warning signs of heat-related illness, which can progress to serious heat stroke if ignored.
During hot months, drink more fluids than usual, avoid outdoor work or travel between late morning and mid-afternoon, wear light cotton clothing, and use ORS or homemade salt-sugar-lemon drinks to stay hydrated, especially for outdoor workers and farmers.
Give extra attention to children, elderly persons, pregnant women, and people with chronic illness during heat waves, as they are more vulnerable to dizziness and heat exhaustion.
Anaemia is common among women and children in many rural areas of Odisha. Eating iron-rich foods and taking iron-folic acid tablets as advised by your ASHA worker or health centre can help reduce dizziness linked to low blood count.
During outbreaks of diarrhoeal illness, dehydration can also cause dizziness and weakness; seek ORS and medical care promptly if dizziness occurs alongside loose motions or vomiting.
Free consultation and referral are available at the nearest Ayushman Arogya Mandir (Health and Wellness Centre), PHC, or Community Health Centre (CHC). ASHA and ANM workers can help guide you to the right facility.
Source Basis
This document is based on general public health guidance and awareness principles published by the World Health Organization (WHO), the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the National Health Mission (NHM), and the Odisha Department of Health and Family Welfare regarding heat-related illness, dehydration, anaemia, and general first-aid and self-care practices. It does not quote or reproduce any specific publication and does not represent official guidance from any single source.
